name: Alginic acid
text:
Alginic acid is a polysaccharide found in brown seaweed. It absorbs water and forms a viscous gum; its salts are known as alginates.

In food it is used mainly as a thickener, stabiliser and gelling agent, and it can also act as an emulsifier, humectant and carrier.

In 2017 EFSA re-evaluated alginic acid and its salts (E400 to E404) and found no safety concern at the reported uses, with no need for a numerical acceptable daily intake.

name: Sodium alginate
text:
Sodium alginate is the sodium salt of alginic acid and the main form in which alginate is extracted from brown seaweed. In water it forms a viscous gum, and adding calcium salts turns the solution into a gel.

It is used as a thickener, stabiliser and gelling agent, for example in drinks, ice cream and jellies, and with soy protein in meat analogues. Cooks use it with calcium for spherification.

In 2017 EFSA re-evaluated alginates (E400 to E404) and found no safety concern at the reported uses.

name: Potassium alginate
text:
Potassium alginate is the potassium salt of alginic acid, a polysaccharide obtained from brown seaweed.

Like the other alginates, it is used in food mainly as a thickener, stabiliser and gelling agent.

In 2017 EFSA re-evaluated alginic acid and its salts (E400 to E404) and found no safety concern at the reported uses.

name: Ammonium alginate
text:
Ammonium alginate is the ammonium salt of alginic acid, a polysaccharide found in brown seaweed. It is a water-soluble white to yellowish-brown powder or granulate.

It is used in food as a thickener, stabiliser, gelling agent and emulsifier.

In 2017 EFSA re-evaluated alginic acid and its salts (E400 to E404) and found no safety concern at the reported uses.

name: Calcium alginate
text:
Calcium alginate is the calcium salt of alginic acid, a polysaccharide from brown seaweed. It is insoluble in water and gelatinous; it forms when a calcium salt such as calcium chloride is added to a sodium alginate solution.

In food it is used as a thickener, stabiliser and gelling agent, and this reaction is the basis of spherification in molecular gastronomy.

In 2017 EFSA re-evaluated alginic acid and its salts (E400 to E404) and found no safety concern at the reported uses.

name: Propylene glycol alginate
text:
Propylene glycol alginate (propane-1,2-diol alginate) is an ester of alginic acid, which comes from brown seaweed (kelp). Part of the acid groups of the alginate are esterified with propylene glycol; the rest are free or neutralised.

It is used as a thickener, stabiliser, emulsifier and foaming agent, for example in frozen dairy desserts, sauces, gravies and condiments.

In the body it is broken down into alginic acid and propylene glycol. EFSA's 2018 re-evaluation set an acceptable daily intake of 55 mg per kg of body weight and found that estimated intakes did not exceed it.

name: Agar
text:
Agar (agar-agar) is a jelly-forming mixture of polysaccharides obtained from the cell walls of certain red seaweeds. It dissolves in boiling water and sets into a gel on cooling, and the gel melts again only at a much higher temperature. It is used as a vegetarian and vegan substitute for gelatin.

It is used as a gelling agent, thickener and stabiliser in jellies, jams, desserts, ice cream, sweets and soups, and is also widely used to make culture media in microbiology.

name: Carrageenan
text:
Carrageenan is a group of sulfated polysaccharides extracted from red seaweeds. The kappa and iota types form gels, kappa reacts with milk proteins, and lambda only thickens.

It is used as a thickener, gelling agent and stabiliser in dairy products such as ice cream, yogurt and chocolate milk, in desserts, processed meats and plant milks.

In its 2018 re-evaluation EFSA found no genotoxicity or carcinogenicity concern but noted data gaps, so it made the acceptable daily intake of 75 mg per kg of body weight temporary. Poligeenan, a degraded low-molecular-weight form, is not used in food.

name: Processed eucheuma seaweed
text:
Processed eucheuma seaweed is semi-refined carrageenan. Red seaweeds such as Eucheuma are washed, cooked in hot alkali, dried and milled without dissolving and filtering out the carrageenan, so the product keeps much more of the seaweed's cellulose than refined carrageenan (E407).

It is used as a thickener, gelling agent and stabiliser, like carrageenan.

EFSA evaluated it together with carrageenan in 2018, and the two share one temporary acceptable daily intake of 75 mg per kg of body weight.

name: Baker's yeast glycan
text:
Baker's yeast glycan is made from the cell walls of baker's yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae), which are ground, washed, pasteurised and dried. It consists mainly of long-chain carbohydrates, glucan and mannan in a ratio of about 2:1.

It is used as a thickener, stabiliser, emulsifier and texturiser in salad dressings, in imitations of frozen desserts, sour cream and cheese spread, and in cheese- and sour-cream-flavoured snack dips.

name: Arabinogalactan
text:
Arabinogalactan (larch gum) is a polysaccharide built from the sugars arabinose and galactose. The food additive is extracted with water from western larch wood and contains roughly six galactose units for every arabinose unit. Arabinogalactans are also a major component of plant gums such as gum arabic.

It is used as an emulsifier, stabiliser, binder and thickener, for example in essential oils, flavour bases, tabletop sweeteners, dressings and pudding mixes.

name: Locust bean gum
text:
Locust bean gum, also called carob gum, is a galactomannan, a polysaccharide of mannose and galactose units, obtained from the seeds of the carob tree, which is native to the Mediterranean. It is a white to yellowish powder that disperses in hot or cold water.

It is used as a thickener, stabiliser and emulsifier.

In 2017 EFSA re-evaluated it and found no need for a numerical acceptable daily intake and no safety concern for the general population at the reported uses. It is barely digested and is fermented by gut bacteria.

name: Oat gum
text:
Oat gum is a plant gum obtained from oats.

It is used as a thickener and stabiliser, increasing the viscosity of foods and helping to keep their texture uniform.

The FAO/WHO expert committee JECFA considered it in 1985 but did not establish an acceptable daily intake or a specification for it.

name: Guar gum
text:
Guar gum is a galactomannan polysaccharide obtained from the seeds of the guar plant; India produces about 80% of the world's supply. It hydrates quickly in cold water and has up to eight times the thickening power of starch.

It is used as a thickener, stabiliser and emulsifier in sauces, dressings, soups, ice cream, yogurt and other dairy products, baked goods and gluten-free products.

In July 2007 the European Commission alerted member states after high levels of dioxins were found in guar gum from India contaminated with the pesticide pentachlorophenol.

name: Tragacanth
text:
Tragacanth is a natural gum obtained from the dried sap of several Middle Eastern shrubs of the genus Astragalus; Iran is the largest producer. It is a mixture of polysaccharides that absorbs water to form a gel or thick paste.

It is used as a thickener, stabiliser and emulsifier. In confectionery it is mixed with sugar to make gum paste for edible decorations, and it is found in some lozenges.

In 2017 EFSA re-evaluated tragacanth and found no need for a numerical acceptable daily intake and no safety concern at the reported uses.

name: Gum arabic
text:
Gum arabic, also called acacia gum, is the dried exudate of certain Acacia trees, harvested mostly in Sudan and across the Sahel. It is a water-soluble mixture of polysaccharides and glycoproteins.

It is used as a stabiliser, emulsifier and thickener, for example to bind sweeteners and flavourings in soft drinks and in icing, fillings, soft candy, gumdrops and chewing gum.

It is fermented in the large intestine; very large doses can cause flatulence. In 2017 EFSA re-evaluated it and found no need for a numerical acceptable daily intake and no safety concern for the general population.

name: Xanthan gum
text:
Xanthan gum is a polysaccharide produced by fermenting sugars such as glucose and sucrose with the bacterium Xanthomonas campestris. Even 1% in a liquid raises its viscosity markedly, and the thickened liquid thins while it is stirred or poured and thickens again at rest.

It is used as a thickener and stabiliser in sauces, salad dressings, ice cream, gluten-free baking, dairy products and drinks.

In its 2017 re-evaluation EFSA found no safety concern for the general population; some people taking large amounts reported abdominal discomfort.

name: Karaya gum
text:
Karaya gum (sterculia gum) is a plant gum that seeps from trees of the genus Sterculia, such as Sterculia urens. Chemically it is an acidic polysaccharide made of galactose, rhamnose and galacturonic acid.

In food it is used as a thickener, stabiliser and emulsifier. Outside food it is used as a laxative and as a denture adhesive.

In 2016 EFSA found no safety concern at the estimated intake from food, but advised that adult intake should stay below 7 g a day, the level at which some people had abdominal discomfort.

name: Tara gum
text:
Tara gum is a galactomannan made by grinding the endosperm of the seeds of the tara tree, native to Peru. It is a white or beige powder. Its solutions are less viscous than guar gum but more viscous than locust bean gum.

It is used as a thickener, stabiliser and gelling agent, for example in ice cream.

In 2017 EFSA found no need for a numerical acceptable daily intake and no safety concern at the reported uses. It is distinct from tara flour, made from the seed germ, which sickened consumers in the US in 2022.

name: Gellan gum
text:
Gellan gum is a polysaccharide produced by fermentation with the bacterium Sphingomonas elodea. It forms clear gels and needs only about half the concentration of agar for the same gel strength; low-acyl types give firm, brittle gels and high-acyl types soft, elastic ones.

It is used as a gelling agent, thickener and stabiliser, for example in vegan gummy sweets as a gelatin substitute and in plant-based milks to keep protein suspended.

In 2018 EFSA found no need for a numerical acceptable daily intake and no safety concern at the reported uses.

name: Gum ghatti
text:
Gum ghatti (Indian gum) is a natural gum that exudes from wounds in the bark of Anogeissus latifolia, a tree of the dry deciduous forests of India and Sri Lanka.

It is used as an emulsifier, stabiliser and thickener, mainly as an emulsifier in soft drinks and drink bases. Outside food it has been used in calico printing.

name: Sorbitol
text:
Sorbitol is a sugar alcohol made by reducing glucose, mostly from starch; it also occurs naturally in apples, stone fruits and berries. E420 covers sorbitol and sorbitol syrup. It is about half as sweet as sugar and provides roughly 2.5 to 3.4 kcal per gram instead of about 4.

It is used as a sweetener, humectant and bulking agent in sugar-free chewing gum, mints, diet foods, biscuits and fruit preserves.

Like other sugar alcohols it can cause digestive upset and acts as a laxative in larger amounts. In the EU, foods with more than 10% added polyols must carry the warning "excessive consumption may produce laxative effects".

name: Mannitol
text:
Mannitol is a sugar alcohol found in almost all plants and in seaweed. It is made industrially by hydrogenating fructose or extracted from seaweed. It raises blood glucose less than sugar and hardly absorbs moisture from the air.

It is used as a sweetener, anti-caking agent, humectant and bulking agent, for example in chewing gum and as a coating for hard sweets and dried fruit.

Oral doses above about 20 g act as a laxative. In the EU, foods with more than 10% added polyols must carry the warning "excessive consumption may produce laxative effects".

name: Glycerol
text:
Glycerol (glycerine) is a colourless, odourless, sweet-tasting, viscous liquid. It is obtained mainly from animal fats and vegetable oils, where it is bound in triglycerides, and can also be made synthetically.

In food it is used as a humectant, solvent, sweetener and thickener, for example as a filler in low-fat biscuits and to thicken liqueurs.

In 2017 EFSA found no safety concern at the reported uses, but noted that infants and toddlers could reach a dose with a therapeutic effect by drinking less than one 330 ml can of a flavoured drink.

name: Octenyl succinic acid modified gum arabic
text:
This additive is gum arabic (acacia gum, E414) that has been chemically modified with octenyl succinic anhydride.

It is used as an emulsifier, mainly in flavour-oil emulsions for flavourings.

In 2010 EFSA concluded that its use as an emulsifier at the proposed uses and levels raised no safety concern, based on its own toxicity data together with data on gum arabic and on starch modified in the same way (E1450). In 2009 JECFA had set a temporary acceptable daily intake for it without a numerical limit.

name: Curdlan
text:
Curdlan is a high-molecular-weight polysaccharide made of glucose units joined by beta-1,3 links. It is produced by fermentation with the bacterium Rhizobium radiobacter, also classed as Agrobacterium; the producing strain was first described as Alcaligenes faecalis. It does not dissolve in water, but a suspension forms an elastic gel when heated.

It is used as a gelling and firming agent, stabiliser and thickener, for example in noodles, processed meat products, fish paste, sauces, soups and processed tofu.

In 2024 EFSA found no safety concern at the proposed uses. Curdlan is not absorbed; gut bacteria break it down, largely to carbon dioxide.

name: Konjac
text:
Konjac (konjac gum and konjac glucomannan) is obtained from the corm of the konjac plant (Amorphophallus konjac). The dried corm is about 40% glucomannan, a water-soluble polysaccharide and dietary fibre that gives firm, elastic jellies.

It is used as a thickener, gelling agent, stabiliser and emulsifier, and is the basis of shirataki noodles and konjac jellies.

In 2003 the EU ruled out konjac in jelly confectionery, including jelly mini-cups, after such sweets caused choking deaths of children and elderly people elsewhere. In 2017 EFSA found no safety concern provided total intake from all sources stays below 3 g a day.

name: Soybean hemicellulose
text:
Soybean hemicellulose is a polysaccharide fraction obtained from soybeans. It is used as an emulsifier, stabiliser, thickener and anti-caking agent.

It is not absorbed intact but is extensively fermented by gut bacteria. In its 2017 re-evaluation EFSA found a safety concern very unlikely and no need for a numerical acceptable daily intake. Because the additive can contain residual soy proteins, EFSA recommended reducing them as far as possible and informing consumers that potentially allergenic proteins may be present.

name: Cassia gum
text:
Cassia gum is made from the endosperm of the seeds of Senna obtusifolia and Senna tora (also called Cassia obtusifolia and Cassia tora). It is at least 75% polysaccharide, mainly a galactomannan with about five mannose units per galactose unit.

It is used as a thickener, gelling agent, stabiliser and emulsifier. It is also used in pet food, where it has the feed additive number E499.

name: Gelatin
text:
Gelatin is a translucent, colourless, nearly flavourless mixture of proteins and peptides made by partial hydrolysis of collagen from the skin, bones and connective tissue of animals, mostly pigs and cattle, sometimes fish. It dissolves in hot water and forms a gel on cooling that melts again when reheated.

It is used as a gelling agent, stabiliser and thickener in jellies, gummy sweets, marshmallows, ice cream, yogurts and capsules.

Being of animal origin, it is not suitable for vegetarians, and pork or beef gelatin raises religious objections for some consumers.

name: Peptones
text:
Peptones are variable mixtures of polypeptides, oligopeptides and amino acids made by partially breaking down proteins such as casein, whey protein, egg albumin, gelatin, animal tissue or soy protein with enzymes, acids or heat.

In food they are used as emulsifiers and surface-active agents, as processing aids and as nutrient supplements. They are also widely used in nutrient media for growing bacteria and fungi.

name: Polyoxyethylene (8) stearate
text:
Polyoxyethylene (8) stearate is a synthetic non-ionic surfactant: an ester of stearic acid, a fatty acid, with a polyethylene glycol chain of about eight oxyethylene units.

In food it is classed as an emulsifier, helping oil and water mix.

The FAO/WHO expert committee JECFA set an acceptable daily intake of 0 to 25 mg per kg of body weight for polyoxyethylene (8) and (40) stearates taken together.

name: Polyoxyethylene (40) stearate
text:
Polyoxyethylene (40) stearate is a synthetic non-ionic surfactant: an ester of stearic acid, a fatty acid, with a polyethylene glycol chain of about forty oxyethylene units.

In food it is classed as an emulsifier, helping oil and water mix.

The FAO/WHO expert committee JECFA set an acceptable daily intake of 0 to 25 mg per kg of body weight for polyoxyethylene (8) and (40) stearates taken together.

name: Polysorbate 20
text:
Polysorbate 20 (polyoxyethylene (20) sorbitan monolaurate) is a synthetic nonionic surfactant made by reacting sorbitan monolaurate, an ester of sorbitol and lauric acid, with ethylene oxide. It acts as an emulsifier, helping oil and water to mix.

In food it is used in small amounts, for example as a wetting agent in flavoured mouth drops. It is also widely used in medicines, cosmetics and laboratory work.

JECFA and EFSA have set a group acceptable daily intake of 25 mg per kg of body weight for polysorbates 20, 40, 60, 65 and 80.

name: Polysorbate 80
text:
Polysorbate 80 (polyoxyethylene (20) sorbitan monooleate) is a synthetic nonionic emulsifier, a viscous yellow liquid made from sorbitol, oleic acid and ethylene oxide.

In ice cream it makes the product smoother and more resistant to melting. It is also used in gelatin desserts and in vitamin preparations, and widely in medicines, vaccines and cosmetics.

JECFA and EFSA have set a group acceptable daily intake of 25 mg per kg of body weight for polysorbates. Laboratory research has suggested that polysorbate 80 may affect gut bacteria in ways that promote intestinal inflammation.

name: Polysorbate 40
text:
Polysorbate 40 (polyoxyethylene (20) sorbitan monopalmitate) is a synthetic nonionic emulsifier made from sorbitol, palmitic acid and ethylene oxide. Like other polysorbates, it helps oil and water to mix. Polysorbates are used, for example, in fine bakery wares, ice cream, desserts, chewing gum and emulsified sauces.

JECFA and EFSA have set a group acceptable daily intake of 25 mg per kg of body weight for polysorbates 20, 40, 60, 65 and 80.

name: Polysorbate 60
text:
Polysorbate 60 (polyoxyethylene (20) sorbitan monostearate) is a synthetic nonionic emulsifier made from sorbitol, stearic acid (usually with some palmitic acid) and ethylene oxide. It helps oil and water to stay mixed.

It is used in whipped toppings, cakes and cake mixes, icings and fillings, confectionery coatings, dressings, ice cream and powdered drink mixes such as hot cocoa.

JECFA and EFSA have set a group acceptable daily intake of 25 mg per kg of body weight for polysorbates 20, 40, 60, 65 and 80.

name: Polysorbate 65
text:
Polysorbate 65 (polyoxyethylene (20) sorbitan tristearate) is a synthetic nonionic emulsifier made by reacting stearic acid with sorbitol and then with ethylene oxide.

It is used in ice cream and other frozen desserts, cakes and cake mixes, whipped toppings, icings and fillings, and coffee whiteners.

JECFA and EFSA have set a group acceptable daily intake of 25 mg per kg of body weight for polysorbates 20, 40, 60, 65 and 80.

name: Pectins
text:
Pectin is a polysaccharide found in the cell walls of plants. Commercially it is extracted mainly from dried citrus peel and apple pomace, by-products of juice production. Amidated pectin is a modified form that needs less calcium to gel and tolerates excess calcium better.

It is the classic gelling agent for jams and jellies, and it is also used as a thickener and stabiliser in dessert fillings, sweets and dairy products.

name: Gelatine
text:
Gelatine is a protein obtained by partial hydrolysis of animal collagen. Most gelatine is made from pork skins, pork and cattle bones, or split cattle hides. It is colourless or slightly yellow and nearly tasteless; a warm solution sets to a gel on cooling and melts again when reheated.

It is used in jellies, most gummy sweets, marshmallows, ice cream, dips and yoghurts. Because it is of animal origin, it is unsuitable for vegetarians and vegans.

name: Ammonium phosphatides
text:
Ammonium phosphatides are a mixture of ammonium salts of phosphorylated glycerides. They are made synthetically or from glycerol and partially hardened vegetable oil, most often rapeseed oil.

They are used mainly in the chocolate industry as an emulsifier, often as an alternative to lecithin.

The acceptable daily intake set by JECFA and the EU Scientific Committee on Food is 30 mg per kg of body weight; EFSA saw no reason to revise it in its 2016 re-evaluation.

name: Brominated vegetable oil
text:
Brominated vegetable oil (BVO) is vegetable oil whose fat molecules have been modified with bromine. Because it is denser than water, it was mixed with lighter citrus flavour oils so that they stayed suspended in soft drinks instead of separating; according to the US FDA, it has been used for this purpose since the 1920s.

In July 2024 the FDA revoked the US rule that allowed BVO in fruit-flavoured drinks, with effect from 2 August 2024. Rodent studies carried out with the US National Institutes of Health had shown that BVO is toxic to the thyroid and that bromine from it builds up in the body.

name: Sucrose acetate isobutyrate
text:
Sucrose acetate isobutyrate (SAIB) is a synthetic ester made by esterifying sucrose with acetic and isobutyric anhydrides.

In drinks it is used as a weighting agent: added to flavour oils, it keeps them evenly dispersed in the drink instead of separating, and it serves as an alternative to brominated vegetable oil. It is also used in cosmetics and as a fragrance fixative.

In its 2016 re-evaluation EFSA set an acceptable daily intake of 20 mg per kg of body weight, the same value JECFA had set in 1997.

name: Glycerol esters of wood rosins
text:
Glycerol esters of wood rosin, also called ester gum, are made by reacting refined wood rosin, for example rosin extracted from aged pine stumps, with glycerol.

They are oil-soluble and are used in drinks to keep flavour oils suspended in the water, notably in citrus-flavoured soft drinks as an alternative to brominated vegetable oil. They are also used in chewing gum and ice cream.

In a 2023 follow-up to its re-evaluation, EFSA found no safety concern at the maximum or reported use levels.

name: Succistearin
text:
Succistearin (stearoyl propylene glycol hydrogen succinate) is a synthetic emulsifier, the reaction product of succinic anhydride, fully hydrogenated vegetable oil and propylene glycol.

US food additive regulations list its use as an emulsifier in shortenings and edible oils used in cakes, cake mixes, fillings, icings, pastries and toppings.

name: Diphosphates
text:
Diphosphates (pyrophosphates) are salts of diphosphoric acid; the additive group covers sodium, potassium, calcium and magnesium diphosphates. Disodium diphosphate, for example, is made by heating sodium dihydrogen phosphate.

They act as raising agents, emulsifiers, stabilisers, acidity regulators, sequestrants and water-retention agents. Disodium diphosphate is a common acid in baking powder, helps cured meats hold water and keeps frozen potato products from darkening.

In 2019 EFSA set a group acceptable daily intake for phosphate additives of 40 mg of phosphorus per kg of body weight and noted that children's estimated total phosphate intake can exceed it.

name: Triphosphates
text:
Triphosphates are the sodium and potassium salts of triphosphoric acid: pentasodium triphosphate (sodium tripolyphosphate, STPP) and pentapotassium triphosphate. Sodium tripolyphosphate is made by heating a mixture of disodium and monosodium phosphate.

In food they are used as emulsifiers and to retain moisture, especially in seafood, meat and poultry. Because this can substantially increase the sale weight of seafood, many governments limit the amounts used. STPP is also widely used in detergents.

In 2019 EFSA set a group acceptable daily intake for phosphate additives of 40 mg of phosphorus per kg of body weight.

name: Polyphosphates
text:
Polyphosphates are salts of long-chain phosphoric acids. The additive group includes sodium, potassium, sodium calcium and calcium polyphosphates.

They are used as emulsifiers, humectants, sequestrants, stabilisers and thickeners. Sodium hexametaphosphate, for example, can be found in cheese powders and imitation cheese, whipped toppings, fish fillets, roast beef, ice cream, breakfast cereals, beer and bottled drinks.

They are not known to pose health risks beyond those of other phosphate sources. In 2019 EFSA set a group acceptable daily intake for phosphate additives of 40 mg of phosphorus per kg of body weight.

name: Potassium polyaspartate
text:
Potassium polyaspartate is the potassium salt of polyaspartic acid, a synthetic polyamide made by heat polymerisation of the amino acid L-aspartic acid.

It is used as a stabiliser in wine. Its many negative charges bind positive ions and strongly inhibit the formation of potassium bitartrate (tartrate) crystals in the bottle, without affecting colour stability or filterability. Typical use levels are 100 to 200 mg per litre.

In 2016 EFSA found no safety concern for this use; in laboratory tests the intact compound was barely digested and not absorbed.

name: Beta-cyclodextrin
text:
Beta-cyclodextrin is a ring-shaped oligosaccharide of seven glucose units, made from starch by enzymatic conversion. The inside of the ring is water-repelling, so it can hold other hydrophobic molecules and form inclusion complexes; this is why cyclodextrins are used in food and pharmaceuticals.

It is poorly absorbed; gut bacteria and enzymes in the colon break it down to maltose and glucose.

In 2016 EFSA kept the acceptable daily intake of 5 mg per kg of body weight and noted that, at reported use levels, it could be exceeded by most population groups in a brand-loyal consumption scenario.

name: Cellulose
text:
Cellulose is the main structural component of plant cell walls; for industrial use it is obtained mainly from wood pulp and cotton. The additive covers microcrystalline cellulose, a refined, partially depolymerised form, and powdered cellulose.

In the diet, cellulose is indigestible insoluble fibre. Microcrystalline cellulose is used as a texturiser, anti-caking agent, fat substitute, emulsifier and bulking agent, and as a filler in tablets and vitamin supplements. Powdered cellulose is used, for example, to stop processed cheese from caking in the package.

In 2018 EFSA concluded that no numerical acceptable daily intake was needed for celluloses and found no safety concern at reported use levels.

name: Methyl cellulose
text:
Methyl cellulose does not occur naturally; it is made by heating cellulose with sodium hydroxide solution and treating it with methyl chloride. It dissolves in cold but not in hot water, and, unusually, its gel sets when hot and melts when cold.

It is used as a thickener and emulsifier in foods, in some meat substitutes to imitate the texture of meat, and in vegetarian drug capsules as an alternative to gelatin. It is also a bulk-forming laxative.

Celluloses are not absorbed and pass through the gut intact. In 2018 EFSA found no safety concern at reported use levels.

name: Ethyl cellulose
text:
Ethyl cellulose is a cellulose derivative in which some of the hydroxyl groups of the glucose units are converted into ethyl ether groups. It is one of the few food-grade film formers and thickeners that do not dissolve in water.

It is used mainly as a thin coating for tablets, capsules and vitamin pills, where it protects the contents from water and controls their release. In food it serves as an emulsifier, binder, thickener and stabiliser.

In 2018 EFSA found no safety concern for celluloses at reported use levels.

name: Hydroxypropyl cellulose
text:
Hydroxypropyl cellulose is a cellulose ether made by treating cellulose with propylene oxide, which attaches hydroxypropyl groups to some of its glucose units. It dissolves in cold water but becomes insoluble above a certain temperature.

In food it is used as a thickener, emulsifier, stabiliser, binder and anti-caking agent. It is also a tablet binder in medicines and is used in eye lubricants and cosmetics.

In 2018 EFSA found no safety concern for celluloses at reported use levels.

name: Low-substituted hydroxypropyl cellulose
text:
Low-substituted hydroxypropyl cellulose (L-HPC) is a cellulose ether carrying only a small number of hydroxypropyl groups.

It is used in food supplements in tablet form, where it helps tablets hold together and break apart (disintegrate) when swallowed.

In 2018 EFSA, drawing on its data for other celluloses, found no safety concern for this use at the proposed levels.

name: Hydroxypropyl methyl cellulose
text:
Hydroxypropyl methyl cellulose (hypromellose, HPMC) is a semi-synthetic cellulose ether that carries both methyl and hydroxypropyl groups and dissolves readily in water.

In food it is an emulsifier, thickening and suspending agent, and a plant-based alternative to animal gelatin, for example in vegetarian capsules. Researchers have investigated it as a gluten substitute in oat bread, since it can trap gas bubbles in dough. It is also used in tablets to control the release of medicines and in artificial tears.

In 2018 EFSA found no safety concern for celluloses at reported use levels.

name: Ethyl methyl cellulose
text:
Ethyl methyl cellulose is a cellulose derivative carrying both ethyl and methyl groups. It can be made by treating cellulose with dimethyl sulfate and ethyl chloride in the presence of an alkali.

It is used as a thickener, foaming agent and emulsifier.

In 2018 EFSA found no safety concern for celluloses at reported use levels.

name: Sodium carboxymethyl cellulose
text:
Carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC, cellulose gum) is made by treating cellulose, usually from wood pulp or cotton, with chloroacetic acid or its sodium salt. It is water-soluble and gives highly viscous solutions.

It is used as a thickener and emulsion stabiliser in ice cream, mayonnaise and drinks, in gluten-free and reduced-fat foods, and to prevent tartrate crystals in wine. It is also found in toothpaste and laxatives.

In 2018 EFSA found no safety concern for celluloses at reported use levels. Possible effects of CMC on gut inflammation and the gut microbiome have been studied, and a 2023 review called for human trials.

name: Ethyl hydroxyethyl cellulose
text: Ethyl hydroxyethyl cellulose, also called ethulose, is a cellulose ether, a chemically modified form of cellulose. In the international numbering system for food additives it is listed as an emulsifier, and it is also used as a laxative.

name: Cross-linked sodium carboxymethyl cellulose
text:
Cross-linked sodium carboxymethyl cellulose (croscarmellose sodium) is made by soaking cellulose in sodium hydroxide and reacting it with sodium monochloroacetate; glycolic acid formed in the process links the chains together. The cross-linking makes it barely soluble in water, but it swells and absorbs many times its weight of water.

This makes it a very effective disintegrant: in tablets, including food supplements, it helps the tablet break apart quickly in the digestive tract.

In 2018 EFSA found no safety concern for celluloses at reported use levels.

name: Enzymatically hydrolysed carboxymethyl cellulose
text:
Enzymatically hydrolysed carboxymethyl cellulose is sodium carboxymethyl cellulose that has been partly broken down by enzymes. Like other modified celluloses, it is used as a thickener and stabiliser in processed foods.

In 2018 EFSA found no safety concern for celluloses at reported use levels.

name: Sodium, potassium and calcium salts of fatty acids
text:
These are the sodium, potassium and calcium salts of fatty acids, mainly palmitic and stearic acid; chemically they are soaps. Sodium stearate, for example, forms when fats are saponified or when stearic acid is neutralised with sodium hydroxide. Calcium stearate, unlike sodium and potassium soaps, is insoluble in water.

They are used in food mainly as emulsifiers.

In the gut they split into fatty acids and the corresponding minerals. In 2018 EFSA concluded that no numerical acceptable daily intake was needed and found no safety concern at reported use levels.

name: Magnesium salts of fatty acids
text:
Magnesium salts of fatty acids, chiefly magnesium stearate, are metallic soaps. Magnesium stearate is made by reacting sodium stearate with magnesium salts or by treating magnesium oxide with stearic acid.

In food it is used as an anti-caking and anti-sticking agent, for example as a release agent in pressed sweets. It is the most commonly used lubricant in tablet making, where it stops powders sticking to the equipment.

In 2018 EFSA concluded that no numerical acceptable daily intake was needed and found no safety concern at reported use levels.

name: Mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids
text:
Mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids are partial esters of glycerol with fatty acids. They occur naturally in small amounts in food fats; industrially they are made by reacting fats or oils with glycerol. Most are made from vegetable oils, but animal fats are sometimes used, which matters to vegetarians and vegans.

They are used as emulsifiers in infant formula, fresh pasta, jams, chocolate, creams and baked goods, and as a fruit coating.

In 2017 EFSA found no need for a numerical acceptable daily intake. A 2024 French observational study found a correlation, but not causation, between higher intake and a 15% higher overall cancer risk.

name: Acetic acid esters of mono- and diglycerides
text:
Acetic acid esters of mono- and diglycerides (acetylated monoglycerides) are monoglycerides modified with one or two acetyl groups. They are made either by reacting edible fats with triacetin or by acetylating monoglycerides directly with acetic anhydride.

They are used as emulsifiers and in edible coatings, and outside food as plasticisers.

In the gut they are expected to break down into normal dietary constituents. In 2020 EFSA found no need for a numerical acceptable daily intake and no safety concern at reported use levels.

name: Lactic acid esters of mono- and diglycerides
text:
Lactic acid esters of mono- and diglycerides (glyceryl-lacto esters of fatty acids) are made from glycerol, lactic acid and fatty acids or edible fats and oils.

They are used in food as emulsifiers and plasticisers.

In the gut they are expected to break down into normal dietary constituents. In 2020 EFSA found no need for a numerical acceptable daily intake and no safety concern at reported use levels.

name: Citric acid esters of mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids
text:
An emulsifier, also known as CITREM. It is made by esterifying glycerol with citric acid and edible fatty acids, or by reacting mono- and diglycerides of edible fatty acids with citric acid.

It is used in infant formula: JECFA found no toxicological concern for this use at concentrations up to 9 g/L. It is also used as an emulsifier in some pharmaceutical and cosmetic products.

In its 2020 re-evaluation, EFSA identified no adverse effects relevant for humans and concluded that no numerical acceptable daily intake was needed.

name: Tartaric acid esters of mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids
text:
An emulsifier made from mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids esterified with tartaric acid, sometimes abbreviated TATEM.

When EFSA re-evaluated it in 2020, it found no published manufacturing method, and a technical reference it cited stated that the substance has no manufacturers and no specific applications. EFSA set an acceptable daily intake for it based on its tartaric acid content.

name: Mono- and diacetyl tartaric acid esters of mono- and diglycerides
text:
An emulsifier commonly called DATEM. It is made by reacting mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids with diacetyl tartaric anhydride, or by esterifying them with tartaric and acetic acids.

It is used mainly in baking, where it strengthens the gluten network in dough, and is added to crusty breads such as rye. It is also used in biscuits, coffee whiteners, ice cream and salad dressings.

In its 2020 re-evaluation, EFSA set an acceptable daily intake based on its tartaric acid content.

name: Mixed acetic and tartaric acid esters of mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids
text:
An emulsifier made from mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids esterified with both acetic acid and tartaric acid, sometimes abbreviated MATEM.

EFSA re-evaluated it in 2020 together with the related esters E472a to E472e and set an acceptable daily intake for it based on its tartaric acid content.

name: Succinylated monoglycerides
text:
A mixture of succinic acid esters of mono- and diglycerides, made by succinylating mono- and diglycerides obtained from edible fats and oils, or by esterifying glycerol directly with fatty acids before succinylation.

It is used as an emulsifier in liquid and plastic shortenings and as a dough conditioner in bread baking. The Codex numbering system also lists it as a stabiliser and sequestrant.

name: Sucrose esters of fatty acids
text:
Sucrose esters of fatty acids are made by esterifying sucrose (sugar) with fatty acids from edible oils or fats. Depending on their composition, they act as oil-in-water or water-in-oil emulsifiers.

They are used in foods such as baked goods, confectionery, chewing gum, frozen dairy desserts and coffee or tea drinks with milk. They are also applied as a surface coating on fruits such as apples, pears and peaches, where they help preserve the fruit by blocking respiratory gases.

EFSA's group acceptable daily intake is 40 mg/kg body weight; in 2023 EFSA reported that estimated intakes exceeded it for many population groups.

name: Sucroglycerides
text:
Sucroglycerides are made by reacting sucrose with an edible oil or fat. The product is a mixture of mono- and diesters of sucrose with fatty acids and mono- and diglycerides. Because the reactants do not mix with water, solvents may be needed in production.

They act as emulsifiers and may be used in dairy drinks, beverage whiteners, ice cream and other dairy desserts, chewing gum, soups, sauces and processed meat.

name: Polyglycerol esters of fatty acids
text:
Polyglycerol esters of fatty acids are made from polyglycerols (short chains of glycerol) and fatty acids from edible oils and fats. They act as emulsifiers and stabilisers.

Uses include emulsifying dry whipped-topping bases and preventing clouding in vegetable and salad oils.

In its 2017 re-evaluation, EFSA noted that they are almost fully broken down into polyglycerols and fatty acids in the gut, found no safety concern at reported uses and saw no need for a numerical acceptable daily intake.

name: Polyglycerol polyricinoleate
text:
Polyglycerol polyricinoleate (PGPR) is an emulsifier made from polyglycerol and interesterified ricinoleic acid from castor oil. It is a yellowish, viscous, strongly fat-soluble liquid.

In chocolate and chocolate coatings it is used at low levels, usually with lecithin, to reduce viscosity so the chocolate flows more easily; this also lets manufacturers use less cocoa butter. It is also used in spreads and salad dressings.

In 2017 EFSA set an acceptable daily intake of 25 mg/kg body weight, higher than the 7.5 mg/kg set by JECFA, based on a newer chronic toxicity and carcinogenicity study.

name: Propane-1,2-diol esters of fatty acids
text:
Propane-1,2-diol esters of fatty acids, also called propylene glycol esters of fatty acids, are mono- and diesters of propylene glycol made with fatty acids from edible fats and oils. They are used as emulsifiers.

In its 2018 re-evaluation, EFSA confirmed an acceptable daily intake of 25 mg/kg body weight expressed as propane-1,2-diol, which corresponds to 80 mg/kg body weight of the additive, and found no safety concern at reported use levels.

name: Lactylated fatty acid esters of glycerol and propane-1,2-diol
text:
A mixture of esters made by reacting edible fats or oils with propylene glycol (propane-1,2-diol) and then lactylating the product, that is, combining it with lactic acid.

It is used as an emulsifier, plasticiser and surface-active agent in food.

name: Thermally oxidised soya bean oil interacted with mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids
text:
An emulsifier known as TOSOM. It is made from about 10% thermally oxidised soya bean oil and 90% mono- and diglycerides of fatty acids, which are made to interact and then deodorised under vacuum at 130 °C.

It is used in fat emulsions intended for frying. In 2018 EFSA found the toxicological data insufficient to support the existing acceptable daily intake, but considered the additive of no safety concern given its limited use.

name: Dioctyl sodium sulfosuccinate
text:
Dioctyl sodium sulfosuccinate (docusate sodium) is a synthetic anionic surfactant. In medicine it is widely used as a stool softener for constipation.

In food it works as a wetting agent, emulsifier, dispersant and solubiliser, for example in dry beverage mixes and gelatin desserts, and to dissolve flavourings in drinks.

name: Sodium stearoyl-2-lactylate
text:
Sodium stearoyl-2-lactylate (SSL) is made by esterifying stearic acid with lactic acid and partially neutralising the product with sodium carbonate or sodium hydroxide. It is a cream-coloured powder or brittle solid.

Its main use is in yeast-raised baked goods, where it strengthens dough and delays staling by keeping the crumb soft. It is also used as an emulsifier in icings, fillings, puddings and non-dairy coffee creamers, where it helps disperse the fat in a hot drink.

name: Calcium stearoyl-2-lactylate
text:
Calcium stearoyl-2-lactylate (CSL) is made by esterifying stearic acid with lactic acid and partially neutralising the product with calcium hydroxide. It is a cream-coloured powder.

Its largest use is in yeast-raised baked goods as a dough strengthener. It softens the crumb less than the sodium salt (E481) but strengthens dough better, so it is preferred in some lean hearth breads. It is also used as a whipping agent in egg whites and whipped vegetable-oil toppings, and in dehydrated potatoes and coffee creamers.

name: Stearyl tartrate
text:
Stearyl tartrate is made by esterifying tartaric acid with commercial stearyl alcohol, which is usually a mixture of stearyl and palmityl alcohols. It consists mainly of diesters. It was used as an emulsifier and flour treatment agent.

In 2020 EFSA could not assess its safety because adequate toxicological data were lacking, and it noted that only two products had been labelled with it since 1996. No business operator offered to supply the missing data, so the EU removed it from its list of food additives with effect from 23 April 2024.

name: Stearyl citrate
text:
Stearyl citrate is an ester of citric acid and stearyl alcohol. It works as an emulsifier and as a sequestrant, binding traces of metals.

JECFA last evaluated it in 1973 and set an acceptable daily intake of 0 to 50 mg/kg body weight.

name: Sodium stearoyl fumarate
text: Sodium stearoyl fumarate is a sodium salt derived from stearic acid and fumaric acid. Its assigned technological function as a food additive is that of an emulsifier, helping fat and water to mix.

name: Calcium stearoyl fumarate
text: Calcium stearoyl fumarate is a calcium salt derived from stearic acid and fumaric acid, the calcium counterpart of E485. Its assigned technological function as a food additive is that of an emulsifier.

name: Sodium lauryl sulfate
text:
Sodium lauryl sulfate (sodium dodecyl sulfate) is an anionic surfactant, best known as the foaming detergent in toothpastes, shampoos and soaps.

In food it is used as an emulsifier and whipping aid, for example in egg whites and in making marshmallows.

name: Ethoxylated mono- and diglycerides
text:
Ethoxylated mono- and diglycerides, also called polyglycerate 60, are made by reacting mono- and diglycerides, mainly of stearic, palmitic and myristic acids, with ethylene oxide.

They are used as emulsifiers, for example in cakes and cake mixes, icings, whipped vegetable-oil toppings and frozen desserts, and as a dough conditioner in yeast-raised baked goods.

name: Methyl glucoside-coconut oil ester
text:
An ester of methyl glucoside, a derivative of glucose, with the fatty acids of coconut oil. It is classed as an emulsifier.

It is used as an aid in the crystallisation of sucrose and dextrose and as a surfactant in molasses.

name: Propylene glycol
text:
Propylene glycol (propane-1,2-diol) is a viscous, colourless, almost odourless liquid with a faintly sweet taste. It mixes with water and many other solvents. Food-grade propylene glycol is made mainly from propylene oxide.

The number E490 was given to it in European rules on additives for animal feed. As a food additive it carries the number E1520 and is used as a humectant and as a solvent and carrier, including in flavourings, other additives and nutrient preparations.

In its 2018 re-evaluation, EFSA kept the acceptable daily intake of 25 mg/kg body weight.

name: Sorbitan monostearate
text:
Sorbitan monostearate is made by reacting stearic acid, usually with some palmitic acid, with sorbitol, giving a mixture of esters of sorbitan, a sorbitol derivative. It is a non-ionic surfactant with emulsifying, dispersing and wetting properties.

It is used as an emulsifier in whipped toppings, cakes and cake mixes, icings and fillings, chocolate and confectionery coatings and coffee whiteners, and as a rehydration aid in active dry yeast.

In 2017 EFSA set a group acceptable daily intake for sorbitan esters (E491 to E495) of 10 mg/kg body weight, expressed as sorbitan.

name: Sorbitan tristearate
text:
Sorbitan tristearate is an ester of sorbitan, a sorbitol derivative, with stearic acid. It is a waxy, light cream to tan non-ionic surfactant.

In food it is used as a dispersing agent, emulsifier and stabiliser.

In 2017 EFSA set a group acceptable daily intake for sorbitan esters (E491 to E495) of 10 mg/kg body weight, expressed as sorbitan.

name: Sorbitan monolaurate
text:
Sorbitan monolaurate is a mixture of esters of lauric acid with polyols derived from sorbitol, including sorbitan and isosorbide. Like other sorbitan esters it is a non-ionic surfactant, used in food as an emulsifier and stabiliser.

In 2017 EFSA set a group acceptable daily intake for sorbitan esters (E491 to E495) of 10 mg/kg body weight, expressed as sorbitan.

name: Sorbitan monooleate
text:
Sorbitan monooleate is an ester of sorbitan, a sorbitol derivative, with oleic acid. Like other sorbitan esters it is a non-ionic surfactant, used in food as an emulsifier and stabiliser.

In 2017 EFSA set a group acceptable daily intake for sorbitan esters (E491 to E495) of 10 mg/kg body weight, expressed as sorbitan.

name: Sorbitan monopalmitate
text:
Sorbitan monopalmitate is an ester of sorbitan, a sorbitol derivative, with palmitic acid. Like other sorbitan esters it is a non-ionic surfactant, used in food as an emulsifier.

In 2017 EFSA set a group acceptable daily intake for sorbitan esters (E491 to E495) of 10 mg/kg body weight, expressed as sorbitan.

name: Sorbitan trioleate
text: Sorbitan trioleate is an ester of sorbitan, a sorbitol derivative, with oleic acid. Like other sorbitan esters it is a non-ionic surfactant; as a food additive its assigned function is that of a stabiliser.

name: Polyoxypropylene-polyoxyethylene polymers
text:
These are synthetic non-ionic block copolymers, also known as poloxamers: a central chain of polyoxypropylene (polypropylene oxide) flanked by two chains of polyoxyethylene (polyethylene oxide). They act as surfactants.

The number E497 comes from European rules on additives for animal feed, where these polymers were listed among emulsifiers and stabilisers; that feed listing was withdrawn in 2017.

In food, polymers of this type have been used as solubilising and stabilising agents in flavour concentrates and as dough conditioners in yeast-raised baked goods.

name: Partial polyglycerol esters of polycondensed fatty acids of castor oil
text:
Partial esters of polyglycerol with polycondensed fatty acids from castor oil, also known as polyglycerol polyricinoleate. As a food emulsifier the same substance has the number E476.

The number E498 comes from European rules on additives for animal feed, where the substance was listed as an emulsifier for dog food; that feed listing was withdrawn in 2017.

name: Stigmasterol-rich plant sterols
text:
A mixture of plant sterols with a high proportion of stigmasterol, one of the most abundant plant sterols, found in oils such as soybean and rapeseed oil.

It is used as a stabiliser in ready-to-freeze alcoholic cocktails. In its 2012 assessment of this use, EFSA noted that less than 5% of dietary plant sterols are absorbed from the gut and concluded that the proposed use would not be of safety concern.
